/.title: Procurement purchase-to-pay (BPI Challenge 2019)
/.problem: Can we predict completion rates and cycle times after a workforce expansion?
/.protocol_line: Model selected on pre-policy validation, refitted through August 31, and scored on September-October prediction windows; subsequent case events are withheld.
/.situation: A multinational's purchase-to-pay operation: purchase-order items are ordered, received, invoiced and cleared in the payment run. In September 2018 the active workforce expanded, and the order mix shifted towards requisition-first items.
/.data_used: The public BPI Challenge 2019 event log: 251,734 purchase-order line items and 1.4 million timestamped steps for all of 2018, with the user who performed each step. Process parameters are selected using January-June fitting and July-August validation, then refitted through August 31.
/.intro: Replays one company's purchase-to-pay operation on an hourly clock: 251,734 purchase-order line items in 2018, worked by 607 specialized users and 20 batch jobs. The simulation continues every live item for two weeks from a Monday cutoff and is scored against what actually happened next, after the September 2018 workforce expansion, with observed pre-change data as reference. The alternatives explore operating without the expansion and adding an AI assistant for invoice entry.
/.world: One multinational company's purchase-order line items for 2018: buyers create orders, vendors invoice, goods are received, accounts payable matches and clears invoices, with payment blocks and rework when documents disagree. 607 specialized human users, 20 batch jobs, vendors as external actors.

narrative.title: Purchase-to-pay, simulated against the real operation
narrative.subtitle: BPI Challenge 2019 procurement log: 251,734 purchase-order items, 607 people, 42 activities. Refitted on January-August 2018, scored on September-October 2018.
takeaways: Before the September 2018 expansion (2018-08-06, 2018-08-13, about 216 active people) 6.8% of live items were completed within 14 days; after it (2018-09-03, 2018-09-17, 2018-10-01, 2018-10-15, about 322 people, 1.49x) reality moved to 13.1% and the simulation predicted 11.8%. Median cycle time: 64 days before; 77 days actual vs 71 days predicted after.

Starting from the observed prefixes of 64,619 live purchase-order items, the simulation's top-ranked next step matched the real next step 81.5% of the time, against 78.4% for the best prefix-Markov baseline (order 1: 70.9%, order 2: 78.4%); log-loss 0.679 vs 0.721.

Over four September-October 2018 cutoffs, 11.8% of live items were completed within 14 days in simulation against 13.1% in reality (training-window history alone would say 11.1%); the simulated median cycle time of completed items was 71 days against 77 days.

The simulated operation produced 23,659 events per week against 29,084 actual, with an activity-mix divergence of 0.009 bits (Jensen-Shannon; 0 is identical) and a rank correlation of 0.83 between simulated and actual median delays on the ten busiest hand-offs.
4.6% of items hit an exception in the horizon (actual 6.0%) and work changed hands 0.44 times per active item (actual 0.46).

The slowest busy hand-offs in the full log are Record Invoice Receipt -> Clear Invoice (median 36 days, p90 91 days) and Remove Payment Block -> Clear Invoice (median 25 days), while the slowest hand-off into goods receipt has a median of 12.8 days; 90% of all clearings happen in the Thursday payment run, and the run in the week of the 24th clears 8x a regular week.

Under the alternative's uniform staffing reduction on the same 12 cutoff-seed runs, 14-day completion moves from 11.8% to 11.8% and the median cycle time from 71 days to 72 days; AP invoice clerks go from 29% to 47% of working-hour capacity. This counterfactual approximates foregoing the expansion; the observed before/after change also includes a different order mix.
Across prediction windows, cases completed within 14 days has mean absolute error 1.35 pp versus 2.47 pp for the strongest non-simulation baseline.
Across prediction windows, median cycle time of completed cases has mean absolute error 127.57 h versus 235.27 h for the strongest non-simulation baseline.

sections.heading: What was simulated
sections.body:
One multinational's purchase-to-pay operation, from the BPI Challenge 2019 event log: 251,734 purchase-order line items on 76,349 purchase orders, 1,595,923 recorded events across 42 activity types, 607 human users, 20 batch jobs and 1,975 vendors over thirteen months.

The simulation was calibrated on the pre-policy history through 2018-08-31 (176,282 items, 909,000 events). It was then started cold at four Monday cutoffs (2018-09-03, 2018-09-17, 2018-10-01, 2018-10-15) with every item live at that moment rebuilt from its history, and ran for 14 days with three random seeds each: 12 runs, 63 seconds each. New items created during the horizon arrive when they really did, but every subsequent step, actor and timing is simulated. On average 64,619 live items and 9,243 arrivals were in play per run.

The test window is deliberately hard: in September 2018 the company changed how it works. Active human users rose from about 270 to about 400 per month, and the share of items that start with a purchase requisition went from 3% to 61%. Model fitting ends before the September change. At each prediction cutoff the simulation sees only the case prefix and active workforce; future arrivals are supplied, but their subsequent events are withheld. Model choices were made on two July-August 2018 validation cutoffs; the test protocol above was then run once.

sections.heading: Business outcomes against non-simulation predictions
sections.body:
Mean absolute errors across the four prediction windows; lower is better. Comparators are carry-forward, the pre-policy historical average, and staffing-scaled carry-forward.

- Cases completed within 14 days: simulation MAE 1.351 pp; best non-simulation MAE 2.467 pp (training average).
- Median cycle time of completed cases: simulation MAE 127.574 h; best non-simulation MAE 235.270 h (training average).
- Cases with at least one exception: simulation MAE 1.456 pp; best non-simulation MAE 1.308 pp (carry forward).
- Hand-offs per active case: simulation MAE 0.025 ; best non-simulation MAE 0.092  (training average).
- Events per week in the horizon: simulation MAE 5424.583 ; best non-simulation MAE 1866.050  (training average).

sections.heading: How faithfully it reproduces the real operation
sections.body:
Next step. For the 48,364 live items per cutoff that really had a next step, the simulation's top-ranked option was the real next activity 81.5% of the time, against 78.4% for the best prefix-Markov model fitted on the same training data (log-loss 0.679 vs 0.721). The gain comes from what a Markov chain cannot see: the process constraints that rule steps out, the item's state (goods received, invoice recorded, block released), how long it has already waited and where the next payment run falls in the calendar.

Flow. 11.8% of live items completed within 14 days in simulation versus 13.1% in reality; the median cycle time of those completions was 71 days simulated versus 77 days actual. The simulated operation produced 23,659 events per week against 29,084 actual, with an activity-mix divergence of 0.009 bits.

Behaviour. 4.6% of items hit at least one of the six core exceptions (actual 6.0%); work changed hands 0.44 times per active item (actual 0.46). Median delays of the ten busiest transitions inside the horizon have a rank correlation of 0.83 with the actual ones.

sections.heading: Where the bottlenecks are
sections.body:
Goods arrive and get booked within days; money moves within months. In the full log the two slowest busy hand-offs are **Record Invoice Receipt -> Clear Invoice** (median 36 days, p90 91 days) and **Remove Payment Block -> Clear Invoice** (median 25 days, p90 92 days). Payment clearing is a weekly run: 90% of all invoice clearings happen on Thursdays, and 18.2% of items go through a payment block that a team of 12 specialists (and batch jobs, 29% of releases) has to lift by hand.

Inside a 14-day test horizon only transitions that complete within the fortnight are observable, so the comparison there is on the fast part of the process: the slowest busy transition is Create Purchase Order Item -> Record Goods Receipt (2.9 days actual, 2.9 days simulated), followed by Record Goods Receipt -> Record Invoice Receipt (2.3 days actual, 2.1 days simulated); the rank correlation of simulated and actual median delays across the ten busiest transitions is 0.83. The ordering is not programmed in: it emerges from the calibrated delays, the Thursday payment run and the capacity of the accounts-payable roles.

sections.heading: What the redesign scenarios show
sections.body:
Each scenario restarts the same operation at every evaluation cutoff with matching arrivals and seeds and changes one thing.

- **What if the company had not expanded its workforce?**: 7,616 items completed in 14 days (-0.1% vs baseline), median cycle time of completions 72 days, 50,536 items still open and 3,239 actions queued at the end, mean wait for a human step 7.0 h, AP invoice clerks at 47% utilization.

Baseline for comparison: 7,623 completed, median cycle 71 days, 50,526 open and 3,220 queued at the end, mean wait 6.0 h, AP invoice clerks at 29%.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body:
Ontology. The organization is a typed graph: 4 organizational units, 7 roles bound to real O*NET occupations, 42 activities each mapped to O*NET detailed work activities, 3 systems with their capabilities, four artifacts and the vendor as an external actor.

- **Buyer / requisitioner** (buyer), O*NET 13-1023.00, 25 active users in the training window
- **Purchasing clerk** (purchasing_clerk), O*NET 43-3061.00, 142 active users in the training window
- **Goods receipt clerk** (goods_receipt), O*NET 43-5071.00, 176 active users in the training window
- **AP invoice clerk** (ap_invoice), O*NET 43-3031.00, 26 active users in the training window
- **AP payment specialist** (ap_payment), O*NET 43-3031.00, 12 active users in the training window
- **ERP batch job** (batch), O*NET 15-1244.00, 14 active users in the training window
- **Vendor (external)** (vendor), external actor, 1,975 vendors

Kernel. An hourly clock drives every item through a scheduler. Each role is a capacity pool (people active in the two weeks before the cutoff times their measured actions per active hour); work beyond capacity or outside working hours waits in a queue and the wait is recorded. 4 process families carry their own transition model (previous and last step plus state flags, backing off to shorter memory when the data is thin), and delay distributions, and an item already waiting at the cutoff has its next step conditioned on the time it has waited; 9 preconditions (goods receipt before clearing, blocks released before payment, consignment never invoiced, deletion ends the item) are enforced by the kernel, which rejected 640 invalid options per run. Invoice clearing follows the company's payment calendar fitted on the training window: the week of the first Thursday on or after the 5th clears 1.3x and the week of the first Thursday on or after the 24th 2.4x the average week, other weeks 0.3x. When a step stays in the same role, the person who did the previous step keeps the item with the probability measured in the training window (62% overall).

Workforce at the first cutoff:
- ap_invoice: 8 people active in the two weeks before t0, 18.9 actions per active hour
- ap_payment: 8 people active in the two weeks before t0, 207.7 actions per active hour (the weekly payment run posts thousands of clearings in a few hours)
- buyer: 80 people active in the two weeks before t0, 4.8 actions per active hour
- goods_receipt: 93 people active in the two weeks before t0, 7.3 actions per active hour
- purchasing_clerk: 87 people active in the two weeks before t0, 7.3 actions per active hour

Policies. Every seat (role) is a swappable policy behind one interface: observe the item, the options the kernel allows and the queue, then choose. The demo runs transparent rule policies with calibrated weights; a seat can be switched to a hosted or local language model in policies/seats.yaml without touching the simulation, and the trace records which decisions were made by which policy.

sections.heading: Exploratory alternative: AI invoice assistant
sections.body:
Use AI to extract invoice details and suggest entries, with human review and correction. Keep observed staffing, incoming orders, matching rules, and payment dates. Assistance changes the human effort needed for invoice entry; the simulation then follows the effect on queues and completion. These are exploratory assumptions applied to the historical operation, not measured AI results from this company.


12 matched simulation comparisons. No observed AI outcome is available.

| Outcome | Current policy | AI alternative | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Human effort for the work performed | 3103.68 hours | 3066.23 hours | -37.45 hours |
| Live items completed in 14 days | 11.79 % | 11.80 % | +0.01 pp |
| Median cycle time of completed items | 1715.75 hours | 1716.72 hours | +0.97 hours |
| Mean wait for human capacity | 6.01 hours | 5.99 hours | -0.02 hours |
| Invoice clerk capacity used | 29.39 % | 26.84 % | -2.55 pp |

All five settings below are editable scenario assumptions, not estimates fitted to procurement outcomes.
Coverage 60%; time saved before review 40%; review effort 15%; correction rate 10%; correction effort 100% of the task's ordinary effort.

Human review and correction are included as expected effort. The model assumes errors are corrected before an entry completes; residual errors, AI operating costs, and training costs are not estimated. It does not shorten vendor delays or payment calendars. Human hours are modeled effort inferred from event throughput, not measured time sheets.


[Noy & Zhang (2023): AI assistance on professional writing tasks](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adh2586). Motivates a task-time assumption; does not estimate invoice-processing effects.

/insights.note: Simulated interviews: every answer is rendered from the agent's own simulated record (profile, traits, states, decisions or queue statistics). Nothing here was said by a real person.

interviews.profile: Purchasing clerk: 92 people simulated (92 active before the cutoff), 6.9 actions per active hour.

qa.question: Why do purchase-order items take as long as they do to clear?
qa.answer: The order side is quick; 13.9% of live items completed within the two weeks, and almost all of the remaining time is the invoice side waiting for receipts and the payment run.

qa.question: What is sitting in your queue right now, and why?
qa.answer: Not much that is ours: utilization is 14%. The 48,241 open items are mostly waiting for a prerequisite step or for the next payment run, not for a free pair of hands. which changes little when the wait is structural.

qa.question: Where does rework come from in your step?
qa.answer: Price and quantity changes after the order is placed, and deleted lines. About 4.8% of items hit an exception in the two weeks; each one sends the item back through a change step before the receipt or invoice can match.

qa.question: Whose work do you wait for, and who waits for you?
qa.answer: I wait for buyers release the requisition before I can create the line; goods receipt and accounts payable wait for me. An active item changes hands about 0.8 times in two weeks, and the batch jobs do the routine transfers in between.

qa.answer: Most of the time is not in our hands: an invoice cannot be cleared until the goods receipt is posted and the amounts match, and many vendors invoice before the goods arrive. We are at 28% of capacity, so the queue is not the bottleneck; the match is.

qa.answer: Clearing only happens in the payment run, so an invoice that is ready on a Tuesday waits for the next run whatever we do. Of the items live at the cutoff, 13.9% cleared within two weeks; the median completed item had been open 70 days. but the calendar did not change.

qa.answer: I wait for the invoice clerks' record and the removal of any block; the vendor waits for me. An active item changes hands about 0.8 times in two weeks, and the batch jobs do the routine transfers in between.

/report.title: Purchase-to-pay, simulated against the real operation
/report.subtitle: BPI Challenge 2019 procurement log: 251,734 purchase-order items, 607 people, 42 activities. Refitted on January-August 2018, scored on September-October 2018.
takeaways: Before the September 2018 expansion (2018-08-06, 2018-08-13, about 216 active people) 6.8% of live items were completed within 14 days; after it (2018-09-03, 2018-09-17, 2018-10-01, 2018-10-15, about 322 people, 1.49x) reality moved to 13.1% and the simulation predicted 11.8%. Median cycle time: 64 days before; 77 days actual vs 71 days predicted after.

Starting from the observed prefixes of 64,619 live purchase-order items, the simulation's top-ranked next step matched the real next step 81.5% of the time, against 78.4% for the best prefix-Markov baseline (order 1: 70.9%, order 2: 78.4%); log-loss 0.679 vs 0.721.

Over four September-October 2018 cutoffs, 11.8% of live items were completed within 14 days in simulation against 13.1% in reality (training-window history alone would say 11.1%); the simulated median cycle time of completed items was 71 days against 77 days.

The simulated operation produced 23,659 events per week against 29,084 actual, with an activity-mix divergence of 0.009 bits (Jensen-Shannon; 0 is identical) and a rank correlation of 0.83 between simulated and actual median delays on the ten busiest hand-offs.
4.6% of items hit an exception in the horizon (actual 6.0%) and work changed hands 0.44 times per active item (actual 0.46).

The slowest busy hand-offs in the full log are Record Invoice Receipt -> Clear Invoice (median 36 days, p90 91 days) and Remove Payment Block -> Clear Invoice (median 25 days), while the slowest hand-off into goods receipt has a median of 12.8 days; 90% of all clearings happen in the Thursday payment run, and the run in the week of the 24th clears 8x a regular week.

Under the alternative's uniform staffing reduction on the same 12 cutoff-seed runs, 14-day completion moves from 11.8% to 11.8% and the median cycle time from 71 days to 72 days; AP invoice clerks go from 29% to 47% of working-hour capacity. This counterfactual approximates foregoing the expansion; the observed before/after change also includes a different order mix.
Across prediction windows, cases completed within 14 days has mean absolute error 1.35 pp versus 2.47 pp for the strongest non-simulation baseline.
Across prediction windows, median cycle time of completed cases has mean absolute error 127.57 h versus 235.27 h for the strongest non-simulation baseline.

sections.heading: What was simulated
sections.body:
One multinational's purchase-to-pay operation, from the BPI Challenge 2019 event log: 251,734 purchase-order line items on 76,349 purchase orders, 1,595,923 recorded events across 42 activity types, 607 human users, 20 batch jobs and 1,975 vendors over thirteen months.

The simulation was calibrated on the pre-policy history through 2018-08-31 (176,282 items, 909,000 events). It was then started cold at four Monday cutoffs (2018-09-03, 2018-09-17, 2018-10-01, 2018-10-15) with every item live at that moment rebuilt from its history, and ran for 14 days with three random seeds each: 12 runs, 63 seconds each. New items created during the horizon arrive when they really did, but every subsequent step, actor and timing is simulated. On average 64,619 live items and 9,243 arrivals were in play per run.

The test window is deliberately hard: in September 2018 the company changed how it works. Active human users rose from about 270 to about 400 per month, and the share of items that start with a purchase requisition went from 3% to 61%. Model fitting ends before the September change. At each prediction cutoff the simulation sees only the case prefix and active workforce; future arrivals are supplied, but their subsequent events are withheld. Model choices were made on two July-August 2018 validation cutoffs; the test protocol above was then run once.

sections.heading: Business outcomes against non-simulation predictions
sections.body:
Mean absolute errors across the four prediction windows; lower is better. Comparators are carry-forward, the pre-policy historical average, and staffing-scaled carry-forward.

- Cases completed within 14 days: simulation MAE 1.351 pp; best non-simulation MAE 2.467 pp (training average).
- Median cycle time of completed cases: simulation MAE 127.574 h; best non-simulation MAE 235.270 h (training average).
- Cases with at least one exception: simulation MAE 1.456 pp; best non-simulation MAE 1.308 pp (carry forward).
- Hand-offs per active case: simulation MAE 0.025 ; best non-simulation MAE 0.092  (training average).
- Events per week in the horizon: simulation MAE 5424.583 ; best non-simulation MAE 1866.050  (training average).

sections.heading: How faithfully it reproduces the real operation
sections.body:
Next step. For the 48,364 live items per cutoff that really had a next step, the simulation's top-ranked option was the real next activity 81.5% of the time, against 78.4% for the best prefix-Markov model fitted on the same training data (log-loss 0.679 vs 0.721). The gain comes from what a Markov chain cannot see: the process constraints that rule steps out, the item's state (goods received, invoice recorded, block released), how long it has already waited and where the next payment run falls in the calendar.

Flow. 11.8% of live items completed within 14 days in simulation versus 13.1% in reality; the median cycle time of those completions was 71 days simulated versus 77 days actual. The simulated operation produced 23,659 events per week against 29,084 actual, with an activity-mix divergence of 0.009 bits.

Behaviour. 4.6% of items hit at least one of the six core exceptions (actual 6.0%); work changed hands 0.44 times per active item (actual 0.46). Median delays of the ten busiest transitions inside the horizon have a rank correlation of 0.83 with the actual ones.

sections.heading: Where the bottlenecks are
sections.body:
Goods arrive and get booked within days; money moves within months. In the full log the two slowest busy hand-offs are **Record Invoice Receipt -> Clear Invoice** (median 36 days, p90 91 days) and **Remove Payment Block -> Clear Invoice** (median 25 days, p90 92 days). Payment clearing is a weekly run: 90% of all invoice clearings happen on Thursdays, and 18.2% of items go through a payment block that a team of 12 specialists (and batch jobs, 29% of releases) has to lift by hand.

Inside a 14-day test horizon only transitions that complete within the fortnight are observable, so the comparison there is on the fast part of the process: the slowest busy transition is Create Purchase Order Item -> Record Goods Receipt (2.9 days actual, 2.9 days simulated), followed by Record Goods Receipt -> Record Invoice Receipt (2.3 days actual, 2.1 days simulated); the rank correlation of simulated and actual median delays across the ten busiest transitions is 0.83. The ordering is not programmed in: it emerges from the calibrated delays, the Thursday payment run and the capacity of the accounts-payable roles.

sections.heading: What the redesign scenarios show
sections.body:
Each scenario restarts the same operation at every evaluation cutoff with matching arrivals and seeds and changes one thing.

- **What if the company had not expanded its workforce?**: 7,616 items completed in 14 days (-0.1% vs baseline), median cycle time of completions 72 days, 50,536 items still open and 3,239 actions queued at the end, mean wait for a human step 7.0 h, AP invoice clerks at 47% utilization.

Baseline for comparison: 7,623 completed, median cycle 71 days, 50,526 open and 3,220 queued at the end, mean wait 6.0 h, AP invoice clerks at 29%.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body:
Ontology. The organization is a typed graph: 4 organizational units, 7 roles bound to real O*NET occupations, 42 activities each mapped to O*NET detailed work activities, 3 systems with their capabilities, four artifacts and the vendor as an external actor.

- **Buyer / requisitioner** (buyer), O*NET 13-1023.00, 25 active users in the training window
- **Purchasing clerk** (purchasing_clerk), O*NET 43-3061.00, 142 active users in the training window
- **Goods receipt clerk** (goods_receipt), O*NET 43-5071.00, 176 active users in the training window
- **AP invoice clerk** (ap_invoice), O*NET 43-3031.00, 26 active users in the training window
- **AP payment specialist** (ap_payment), O*NET 43-3031.00, 12 active users in the training window
- **ERP batch job** (batch), O*NET 15-1244.00, 14 active users in the training window
- **Vendor (external)** (vendor), external actor, 1,975 vendors

Kernel. An hourly clock drives every item through a scheduler. Each role is a capacity pool (people active in the two weeks before the cutoff times their measured actions per active hour); work beyond capacity or outside working hours waits in a queue and the wait is recorded. 4 process families carry their own transition model (previous and last step plus state flags, backing off to shorter memory when the data is thin), and delay distributions, and an item already waiting at the cutoff has its next step conditioned on the time it has waited; 9 preconditions (goods receipt before clearing, blocks released before payment, consignment never invoiced, deletion ends the item) are enforced by the kernel, which rejected 640 invalid options per run. Invoice clearing follows the company's payment calendar fitted on the training window: the week of the first Thursday on or after the 5th clears 1.3x and the week of the first Thursday on or after the 24th 2.4x the average week, other weeks 0.3x. When a step stays in the same role, the person who did the previous step keeps the item with the probability measured in the training window (62% overall).

Workforce at the first cutoff:
- ap_invoice: 8 people active in the two weeks before t0, 18.9 actions per active hour
- ap_payment: 8 people active in the two weeks before t0, 207.7 actions per active hour (the weekly payment run posts thousands of clearings in a few hours)
- buyer: 80 people active in the two weeks before t0, 4.8 actions per active hour
- goods_receipt: 93 people active in the two weeks before t0, 7.3 actions per active hour
- purchasing_clerk: 87 people active in the two weeks before t0, 7.3 actions per active hour

Policies. Every seat (role) is a swappable policy behind one interface: observe the item, the options the kernel allows and the queue, then choose. The demo runs transparent rule policies with calibrated weights; a seat can be switched to a hosted or local language model in policies/seats.yaml without touching the simulation, and the trace records which decisions were made by which policy.

sections.heading: Exploratory alternative: AI invoice assistant
sections.body:
Use AI to extract invoice details and suggest entries, with human review and correction. Keep observed staffing, incoming orders, matching rules, and payment dates. Assistance changes the human effort needed for invoice entry; the simulation then follows the effect on queues and completion. These are exploratory assumptions applied to the historical operation, not measured AI results from this company.


12 matched simulation comparisons. No observed AI outcome is available.

| Outcome | Current policy | AI alternative | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Human effort for the work performed | 3103.68 hours | 3066.23 hours | -37.45 hours |
| Live items completed in 14 days | 11.79 % | 11.80 % | +0.01 pp |
| Median cycle time of completed items | 1715.75 hours | 1716.72 hours | +0.97 hours |
| Mean wait for human capacity | 6.01 hours | 5.99 hours | -0.02 hours |
| Invoice clerk capacity used | 29.39 % | 26.84 % | -2.55 pp |

All five settings below are editable scenario assumptions, not estimates fitted to procurement outcomes.
Coverage 60%; time saved before review 40%; review effort 15%; correction rate 10%; correction effort 100% of the task's ordinary effort.

Human review and correction are included as expected effort. The model assumes errors are corrected before an entry completes; residual errors, AI operating costs, and training costs are not estimated. It does not shorten vendor delays or payment calendars. Human hours are modeled effort inferred from event throughput, not measured time sheets.


[Noy & Zhang (2023): AI assistance on professional writing tasks](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adh2586). Motivates a task-time assumption; does not estimate invoice-processing effects.

/scenarios/baseline.title: Baseline, as operated in September 2018
/scenarios/baseline.description: Continue the real operation from Monday 3 September 2018 for 14 days. Every purchase-order line item that was live at that moment is rebuilt from its history; the 10,000 or so items created during the two weeks arrive exactly when they did in reality, but all of their subsequent steps are chosen by the simulated roles. Staffing is the workforce actually active in the two weeks before the cutoff. No interventions.

/scenarios/no_expansion.title: What if the company had not expanded its workforce?
/scenarios/no_expansion.description: This scenario approximates foregoing the expansion by staffing every human role at 62.5% of the workforce observed before each prediction period. It uses the same incoming orders, process constraints and payment-run calendar. The uniform staffing multiplier is a scenario assumption; the simulation estimates how completion, waiting and utilization respond to that assumption.
/scenarios/no_expansion.summary: Approximate foregoing the expansion by staffing every human role at 62.5% of its observed level; explore the effect on completion and utilization.

/scenarios/ai_assistant.title: What if invoice clerks used an AI assistant?
/scenarios/ai_assistant.description: Use AI to extract invoice details and suggest entries, with human review and correction. Keep observed staffing, incoming orders, matching rules, and payment dates. Assistance changes the human effort needed for invoice entry; the simulation then follows the effect on queues and completion. These are exploratory assumptions applied to the historical operation, not measured AI results from this company.
/scenarios/ai_assistant.summary: Assist invoice entry while people review the output; explore handling effort, queueing, and completion.

exploration.note: Human review and correction are included as expected effort. The model assumes errors are corrected before an entry completes; residual errors, AI operating costs, and training costs are not estimated. It does not shorten vendor delays or payment calendars. Human hours are modeled effort inferred from event throughput, not measured time sheets.
